subChunks.title: Self-paced orientation: Foundation
subChunks.hookHtml: This orientation turns a large subject into a manageable plan: learn the language first, then build explanations layer by layer.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core lesson

Psychology rewards steady sequencing. In this phase you build the vocabulary, biological background, cognitive models, and basic research habits that later topics depend on.

Key ideas

  • Treat the phase as a map, not a race.
  • Keep a learning journal with definitions, examples, and uncertainties.
  • Use retrieval practice after each module before starting the next.

How to study this module

Read the lesson once, then close it. Try to rebuild the explanation in your own words before you check the notes. Psychology becomes useful when you can move between definition, example, evidence, and limitation.

subChunks.title: Module 1a: What is Psychology?
subChunks.hookHtml: Psychology begins with a deceptively simple question: how can behaviour and mental life be studied scientifically?
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core lesson

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. It grew from philosophy, physiology, and medicine, but became distinctive when psychologists began testing claims with observation, measurement, and experiment.

Key ideas

  • Early structuralists tried to analyse conscious experience; functionalists asked what mental processes do.
  • Modern psychology studies observable behaviour, cognition, emotion, development, biology, and social life.
  • A psychological explanation should be testable, evidence-based, and open to revision.

How to study this module

Read the lesson once, then close it. Try to rebuild the explanation in your own words before you check the notes. Psychology becomes useful when you can move between definition, example, evidence, and limitation.

Open your notes and write the following. Each line has a purpose: it turns the idea into something you can retrieve and use later.

  1. Step 1: Write a one-sentence definition of psychology.
  2. Step 2: Add two examples: one visible behaviour and one internal mental process.
  3. Step 3: Write why psychology needs scientific methods rather than common sense alone.

Why you are writing it

The learner is separating the subject matter from the method: psychology studies people, but it does so by making claims testable.

subChunks.title: Module 1b: Major Perspectives
subChunks.hookHtml: The major perspectives are different lenses. None explains everything, but each reveals something important that the others can miss.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core lesson

Psychological perspectives organise explanations. Behaviourism focuses on learning from consequences, cognitive psychology on information processing, biological psychology on nervous-system mechanisms, psychodynamic theory on unconscious conflict, humanistic psychology on growth and meaning, and evolutionary psychology on adaptive pressures.

Key ideas

  • Perspectives are tools, not teams to join permanently.
  • The same behaviour can be explained at several levels at once.
  • Good psychological thinking asks which lens fits the evidence and the question.

How to study this module

Read the lesson once, then close it. Try to rebuild the explanation in your own words before you check the notes. Psychology becomes useful when you can move between definition, example, evidence, and limitation.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided lesson: what to write

Open your notes and write the following. Each line has a purpose: it turns the idea into something you can retrieve and use later.

  1. Step 1: Make a six-row table: behaviourist, cognitive, biological, psychodynamic, humanistic, evolutionary.
  2. Step 2: For each row, write what that perspective looks for first.
  3. Step 3: Use the same behaviour, such as exam anxiety, and write one explanation from each lens.

Why you are writing it

Writing parallel explanations trains flexible thinking and prevents the common mistake of treating one perspective as the whole truth.

subChunks.title: Module 1c: Critical Thinking
subChunks.hookHtml: Psychology is full of attractive explanations. Critical thinking is how you stop an attractive explanation from becoming an unearned belief.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core lesson

Critical thinking means evaluating claims by evidence, logic, methods, and alternative explanations. In psychology this includes spotting cognitive biases, distinguishing correlation from causation, checking sample quality, and asking whether a claim could be tested or falsified.

Key ideas

  • Correlation means variables move together; it does not prove one caused the other.
  • Biases such as confirmation bias and availability bias make weak evidence feel strong.
  • Scientific scepticism is active curiosity, not automatic dismissal.

How to study this module

Read the lesson once, then close it. Try to rebuild the explanation in your own words before you check the notes. Psychology becomes useful when you can move between definition, example, evidence, and limitation.

Open your notes and write the following. Each line has a purpose: it turns the idea into something you can retrieve and use later.

  1. Step 1: Write the claim: "People who use social media more are lonelier."
  2. Step 2: List three explanations: social media causes loneliness, loneliness causes more social media use, and a third variable affects both.
  3. Step 3: Write what kind of study would help separate those explanations.

subChunks.title: Module 1d: Ethics in Psychology
subChunks.hookHtml: Psychology studies real people, often at vulnerable moments. Ethics is not paperwork around the science; it is part of the science.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core lesson

Ethical psychology protects participants through informed consent, confidentiality, the right to withdraw, debriefing, risk assessment, and independent review. Famous failures such as Milgram-style distress, Stanford Prison Experiment harms, and deception without proper safeguards show why ethical committees exist.

Key ideas

  • Consent must be informed, voluntary, and ongoing.
  • Confidentiality protects participants from social, legal, or personal harm.
  • Ethics committees weigh scientific value against participant risk before a study begins.

How to study this module

Read the lesson once, then close it. Try to rebuild the explanation in your own words before you check the notes. Psychology becomes useful when you can move between definition, example, evidence, and limitation.

subChunks.title: Pathway 1 Outcome: Foundations Language
subChunks.hookHtml: This checkpoint asks whether you can speak the basic language of psychology accurately and cautiously.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core lesson

By the end of the first pathway, you should be able to define psychology, compare major perspectives, question evidence, and explain why ethics is central to research.

Key ideas

  • Use perspectives flexibly.
  • Separate evidence from interpretation.
  • Treat ethics as a design requirement.

How to study this module

Read the lesson once, then close it. Try to rebuild the explanation in your own words before you check the notes. Psychology becomes useful when you can move between definition, example, evidence, and limitation.
